This paper introduces the TAR model, a new framework that integrates linear and nonlinear components to model the conditional intensity of a discrete-time Poisson process. Distinguishing itself from existing nonlinear models, the TAR's nonlinear component remains constrained to specific intervals of the lagged conditional intensity. We develop a conditionally unbiased recursive estimator for the model's parameters and prove the almost sure consistency of this estimator under specific conditions, which are subsequently used to derive asymptotic normality. The conditions required for almost sure consistency are relatively lenient, allowing the estimator to remain consistent even when the component of the intensity driven by the recent history of the process follows a complex, unknown nonlinear pattern. The utility of the model, its estimator, and the associated asymptotic results are illustrated using a daily dataset of U.S. airline passenger numbers and a weekly dataset of Twitter mentions for the term "Trump." Additionally, we introduce a stepwise method for selecting the optimal order of the TAR model, accompanied by theoretical justification. Finally, we propose a data-driven approach for determining the nonlinear component's domain of action and provide an asymptotically justified significance test to validate this selection. Simulation studies are included to assess the performance of both the model selection criteria. The proposed model, estimator, and selection procedures are also applied to a daily dataset of earthquakes and a weekly dataset of cyberattacks. This presentation reports on selected LHC experiments aimed at exploring the properties of tiny nuclear systems, ranging from proton-proton to heavy-ion collisions. Given that larger systems have already been extensively studied at the LHC, the focus here shifts to specific topics within this established domain, alongside areas uniquely accessible through small-system heavy-ion investigations. The talk also highlights upcoming small-system heavy-ion experiments at other accelerators. Ultimately, the extent of collective behavior in these minimal systems will help define the lower limit for the onset of hydrodynamics, potentially revealing the smallest possible system where such behavior occurs. Furthermore, this analysis will offer insights into what constitutes a truly "small" system for particle production at LHC energies. While hydrodynamics provides a compelling framework for describing collective flow in large systems, it is by no means the only relevant model; therefore, an effective field theory perspective will also be examined for these systems. We analyze the variable-time intervals between X-ray flares in high-mass X-ray binary transients, which consist of a neutron star and a companion star on the main sequence. These intervals exhibit an approximate constant component and an approximate periodic component. We argue that the constant part originates from the system's "repetition interval," defined as the time required for the neutron star to detect a new flare generated by the companion star. This detection mechanism implies that the flares in the companion star's atmosphere are likely global thermal instants (X-ray bursts) occurring at its rear hemisphere. Consequently, the repetition interval corresponds to the interval between these bursts and relies on the relative orbital motion of the two stars along the binary orbit. This dependence allows us to determine the companion star's mean mass-loss rate, a crucial parameter for understanding how mass is transferred to the neutron star and regulating the transient activity. Applying this model to the variable-time interval data for known X-ray binary transients, we predict the repetition intervals for six systems with incomplete time-series data. For the Galactic Centre three-candidate dormant X-ray binaries, we utilize the same analysis method based on the variable-time interval data to conclude that their interburst intervals exceed one year, implying that their mass-loss rates are correspondingly low. Furthermore, we propose that, similar to the six known transients, the Galactic Centre dormant systems will eventually exhibit flaring activity if the companion star of at least one continues to experience mass-loss surges. This prediction offers a testable hypothesis for distinguishing between the three Galactic Centre dormant X-ray binary candidates and a potential criterion for identifying additional systems among the ~50 compact object candidates in the region. Specifically, a sufficient condition for a system to become an X-ray binary transient is the presence of a main-sequence companion star capable of losing mass. Finally, we address a recent claim suggesting that the flares in the neutron star transient XRB "Swift J1756.5−2014" do not support the burst model; we demonstrate that this assertion rests on an incorrect assumption regarding the accretion disk's role in these flares. Additionally, we respond to the suggestion that the X-ray flare activity in the hydrogen-rich X-ray transient "4XCS J230253.1+480341" indicates a merger between a compact object and a main-sequence star, arguing instead that this system's activity can be explained without invoking any special exotic phenomena.

Bipartite vertex splitting, a non-monotone graph transformation where a vertex is removed and its neighbors are connected to a new vertex, is an open problem first posed by Froese, Schultens, and Schultens. They demonstrated that if two graphs share identical spectra (the sets of eigenvalues for their adjacency matrices), then their bipartite vertex divisions—where split vertices in each graph are linked by an edge—also share the same spectrum. This paper introduces an FPT algorithm for completing bipartite vertex divisions when the target graph is fixed. Applying this approach, we resolve the problem for complete divisions of a 5-regular graph. Additionally, we establish that a 6-regular graph $G$ has at most five non-isomorphic bipartite vertex completions $H$ that are cospectral with $G$, and we provide a method to verify this claim for a specific graph family. We conclude by offering a general algorithm to determine all non-isomorphic bipartite vertex completions for any given graph. The core concept driving this work is meticulously analyzing a graph's spectrum alongside its modularity defined by eigenvalue multiplicities.

Extra-large scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems leverage the semi-deterministic characteristics of wireless channels to create an efficient packet-level protocol known as spatial multiplexing access (SMA). By enabling simultaneous transmissions from multiple users within their respective visible areas, SMA enhances spectrum efficiency. Using geometric probability, we derive closed-form expressions for NIA under Poisson-distributed user distributions.
